rows.title: Eyes
rows.text: A review states that in land snails and slugs the optics cannot produce a focused image on the shallow retina, so if you are one, you very likely see no sharp image. If you are a periwinkle, the same kind of review states that the lens of Littorina forms a sharp image on the retina, and if you are a nudibranch, a natural history account says your small eyes sit deep inside your body and tell light from dark without seeing images. Nobody has counted how many eyes you have.
rows.note: No record gives an eye count for any species, so the count is stated as unknown.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a garden snail or one of most other land snails and slugs. A review of the eyes of land snails and slugs finds they are likely to measure only the average light over wide angles, and they are unlikely to resolve fine detail. A compilation of mollusk measurements lists a smallest resolvable angle of about 50 degrees for the slug Arion rufus, so if you are a black slug or a Spanish slug, you very likely see about that coarsely.
rows.note: R4's quote does not state a usable value, so the periwinkle figure was left out. R1's quote does not say what the 52 degrees measures, so I called it a smallest resolvable angle only as the compilation's context implies; please check.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: If you are a Turkish snail, your eye senses light best near 495 nanometers, and an abstract states that both of your two kinds of cell peak between 465 and 500 nanometers. If you are a Limax slug, your genus has four light-sensing proteins that peak between about 455 and 500 nanometers, and the eye of Limax valentianus senses light best near 480. Nobody has measured the eyes of most other snails and slugs.
rows.note: Removed "reports", rounded 496 to 495, and dropped the color-discrimination claim and the blue-green label since no record states them. Left out how the Limax proteins are arranged across cells.

rows.title: Light without eyes
rows.text: If you are the slug Limax valentianus, you still crawl to the dark end of a chamber when you have no eye stalks, as a summary of one study describes. If you are a great pond snail, an abstract states that you have light-sensing cells in the skin of your foot, in your mantle cavity and around your breathing opening. For nearly every other snail and slug, nobody has measured whether you sense light through your skin.
rows.note: Left out R2's shadow withdrawal because its quote only supports skin photoreceptors. Avoided the word "reports" per the voice check.

rows.title: Shadows
rows.text: If you are a great pond snail, a shadow falling across you makes you withdraw. Your skin senses the change in light, with light-sensing cells located mostly on your foot, inside your mantle cavity and in the skin around your breathing pore.
rows.note: R1's value text is cut off; I used only the withdrawal at a shadow and the three body sites stated in the quote.

rows.title: Sea slugs
rows.text: If you are the sea slug Berghia stephanieae, you go straight to a black stripe set outside the arena where you are placed. A meeting abstract describes this test and says you did it reliably.
rows.note: R1's value is cut off at a second stripe test ("isolumin..."), and the quote does not state it, so I left it out. I also left out other sea slugs, since no record covers them. I replaced "reports" because of the voice check.

rows.title: Chitons
rows.text: If you are a West Indian fuzzy chiton, the lenses in your ocelli let them work as small camera eyes. If you are a West Indian green chiton, nobody has measured how sharply you see.
rows.note: Left out the 9–12 figure: R1's quote gives no unit, and the trait is labeled cycles per degree, which would not fit an angular resolution. Please confirm the unit (likely degrees) before a number is added.

rows.title: Sea snails
rows.text: If you are a strawberry conch, you see about 1 cycle per degree, which is about a thirtieth of the 30 cycles per degree a human reads on an eye chart. If you are a common periwinkle, a review lists an estimate for Littorina, your genus, made from the anatomy of its eye, and you very likely have the sharpness of that genus.
rows.note: I left out R2's value (0.113): the quoted table line does not state it, so the periwinkle half gives no figure.

rows.title: Smell
rows.text: If you are a leopard slug, you can find your way back to your resting spot from more than 90 centimeters away by smell, moving upwind. You do not need to follow your own slime trail or use vision to do it. For almost every other snail and slug, nobody has measured what you can smell or from how far.
rows.note: Left out R2 (sea slugs): its quote only says oral tentacles "probably" sense chemicals and does not mention rhinophores.
